Week 7 Overview

The Purpose of This Week

Weeks 1–6 built your knowledge, consolidated it, and prepared your exam technique. Week 7 does three things:

  1. Integration (Days 1–2): Apply TOGAF as a complete, flowing methodology — not isolated facts — through a fully worked end-to-end scenario covering all ADM phases and all 4 architecture domains for a realistic organization.

  2. Examination (Days 3 and 6): Two full 40-question timed practice exams at real exam difficulty and weight distribution. These are the most important two study sessions of your entire 8-week programme.

  3. Gap Closure (Days 4–5 and 7): A structured self-analysis process to identify exactly which topics you are weakest on, combined with targeted re-study guidance. The gap analysis after Exam 1 drives your Day 5 re-study. The gap analysis after Exam 2 drives your Week 8 final focus.

Study Schedule

Day Topic Time

Tuesday Full 4-Domain Architecture — same scenario, all domains, artifacts, governance 3 hours
Wednesday Practice Exam 1 — 40 questions, 55 minutes, timed, no notes 3 hours

Week 7 Targets

  • After Practice Exam 1: Diagnose your weakest topic area; aim for 65%+ (26/40)
  • After Practice Exam 2: Score 75%+ (30/40); this is the threshold for Week 8 readiness
  • If you score below 75% on Exam 2: Identify remaining gaps; Week 8 starts with targeted remediation before the final mock

Days 1–2 (Monday–Tuesday): Full Integrated Scenario

How to Use These Two Days

Days 1 and 2 present a single organization scenario — Al-Noor Digital Health, a Saudi healthcare company undergoing a major digital transformation. Day 1 walks through all 9 ADM phases for this scenario. Day 2 deepens the 4 architecture domains with artifacts and governance decisions.

Why this matters: The exam tests isolated facts, but understanding TOGAF as a flow — where each phase builds on the previous, where documents carry forward, where governance intersects — is what turns a borderline pass into a confident pass. Scenario questions become far easier once you have seen the whole picture once.

How to read this: This is a guided walk-through, not a quiz. Read actively. After each phase, pause and ask: "Could I explain what happened in this phase and why, without looking at the notes?"

The Scenario: Al-Noor Digital Health

Organization: Al-Noor Digital Health (ANDH) — a mid-sized Saudi healthcare company
Headquarters: Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
Operations: 12 hospitals and 45 clinics across KSA
Size: 8,000 employees; 2 million patient records
Current state: A patchwork of 28 different IT systems acquired over 20 years; no enterprise architecture practice; no integration standards; patient data stored in 6 separate, non-connected systems
Transformation goal: Become a fully integrated digital health provider; comply with SAMA and MOH regulations; enable a unified patient record accessible to all care providers; launch a patient-facing mobile app
Timeline: 3-year transformation programme
Regulatory context: Saudi Ministry of Health (MOH) regulations require patient data to remain within KSA borders; NDMO (National Data Management Office) requires data classification and governance

Day 1: ADM Walk-Through — All 9 Phases

Preliminary Phase

What is happening: ANDH's CEO and CIO commission the EA team to "set up an architecture practice and define how we will govern technology decisions before the transformation begins."

Key activities:

  • The EA team assesses ANDH's current Architecture Capability: no EA practice exists → Maturity Level 0 (None)
  • Target maturity: Level 3 (Defined) by end of year 1 — formal ADM processes, Architecture Board established, repository in place
  • TOGAF is tailored to ANDH's context: Arabic/English bilingual documentation; phase sequence retained; terminology aligned with Saudi government standards ("Architecture Review Committee" instead of "Architecture Board")
  • Architecture Principles are established, including:
    • "Patient Data Sovereignty" — all patient data must be processed and stored within KSA borders
    • "Single Patient Record" — every patient has one master record; no duplicates
    • "Technology Independence" — architecture decisions are not driven by existing vendor relationships
    • "Reuse Before Buy Before Build" — prefer existing assets, then procure, then develop custom
  • Architecture Governance setup: Architecture Review Committee (ARC) formed with representation from Clinical, IT, Finance, and Compliance
  • Tailored Architecture Framework documented

Key TOGAF concepts in play:

  • Architecture Capability establishment
  • Tailored Architecture Framework as the output
  • Architecture Principles with Name, Statement, Rationale, and Implications (4 components)
  • Architecture governance structure

What is produced:

  • Tailored Architecture Framework
  • Architecture Principles (4 principles documented)
  • Architecture Review Committee charter
  • Architecture Repository initialized (6 layers created, currently empty)

Phase A: Architecture Vision

What triggers it: The CEO formally submits a Request for Architecture Work to the EA team: "Define the target enterprise architecture for ANDH's 3-year digital transformation."

Key activities:

  • Stakeholders are identified and mapped:
    • High influence, high interest: CEO, CIO, Chief Medical Officer → manage closely
    • High influence, low interest: CFO, Board of Directors → keep satisfied (focus on cost and risk)
    • Low influence, high interest: Clinical staff, IT team, patients → keep informed
  • Stakeholder concerns documented:
    • CEO: "How does this transformation deliver business value and competitive positioning?"
    • CMO: "How will this improve clinical outcomes and patient safety?"
    • CFO: "What does this cost, over what timeframe, and what is the ROI?"
    • CISO: "How do we ensure patient data is protected and compliant with MOH regulations?"
  • Scope defined: Enterprise-wide; all 12 hospitals and 45 clinics; all 28 existing systems in scope for assessment; 3-year horizon
  • Architecture Vision produced: "ANDH will become a fully integrated digital health provider with a unified patient record, AI-assisted clinical decision support, and a patient-facing mobile experience — while maintaining full regulatory compliance with Saudi MOH and NDMO requirements."
  • Statement of Architecture Work produced and approved by CEO (Architecture Sponsor)
  • Initial Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS) created with high-level requirements:
    • Patient data must remain in KSA (regulatory constraint)
    • System availability: 99.9% for clinical systems (non-functional requirement)
    • Unified Patient Record accessible within 3 seconds (performance requirement)
    • All systems must integrate via standardized APIs (architecture requirement)

Key TOGAF concepts in play:

  • Request for Architecture Work → triggers Phase A
  • Stakeholder Map with influence/interest classification
  • Concern → Viewpoint → View chain (CEO's business value concern will drive a Business Footprint Diagram)
  • Architecture Vision ≠ Target Architecture (high-level aspiration, not detailed design)
  • Statement of Architecture Work = governs the architecture development; approved by Architecture Sponsor
  • ARS as a living document starting here

What is produced:

  • Architecture Vision
  • Statement of Architecture Work (approved by CEO)
  • Stakeholder Map and Register
  • Initial Architecture Requirements Specification

Phase B: Business Architecture

What is happening: The architect team designs ANDH's Target Business Architecture — what the business must look like in 3 years to achieve the Vision.

Baseline Business Architecture (AS-IS):

  • Capabilities identified: Clinical Care Delivery, Patient Registration, Appointment Management, Pharmacy Management, Laboratory Services, Billing & Finance, Workforce Management — all operating independently with no integration
  • Capability gaps identified against Vision: No "Unified Patient Record Management" capability; no "Digital Patient Engagement" capability; no "Clinical Decision Support" capability
  • Process issues: Patient registration is performed independently in each hospital — a patient visiting Hospital A and Clinic B has two separate records, no shared history
  • Organizational gap: No Chief Digital Officer role; no Data Governance function

Target Business Architecture (TO-BE):

  • New capabilities: "Unified Patient Record Management," "Digital Patient Engagement" (mobile app), "Clinical Decision Support," "Population Health Analytics"
  • New roles: Chief Digital Officer, Data Governance Officer, Patient Data Steward
  • Revised process: Centralized patient registration with a Master Patient Index as the single authoritative source
  • New business service: "Unified Clinical Portal" — clinicians access all patient data from one interface

Gap Analysis (Phase B):

Gap Classification Description
Unified Patient Record Management Added Does not exist; must be created
Digital Patient Engagement Added No mobile app or patient portal; must be created
Clinical Decision Support Added No AI/analytics capability; must be created
Manual patient registration per facility Eliminated Must be replaced by centralized registration
Chief Digital Officer role Added Role does not exist; must be staffed
Data Governance Officer role Added Role does not exist; must be staffed

Business Motivation Model documented:

  • Vision: "Become the leading integrated digital health provider in KSA"
  • Goal: "Deliver seamless, data-driven patient care across all ANDH facilities"
  • Objective: "Achieve unified patient record access across 100% of facilities by end of Year 2"
  • Mission: "Provide safe, accessible, world-class healthcare to patients across Saudi Arabia"
  • Strategy: "Build a unified digital infrastructure that connects all clinical systems and patient touchpoints"

Key TOGAF concepts in play:

  • 9-step Phase B pattern (baseline → target → gap analysis → roadmap components → stakeholder review → finalize → update ADD)
  • Business Capability Map showing existing and new capabilities
  • Business Footprint Diagram connecting CEO's business value concern to capabilities to services
  • Business Function/Organization Matrix revealing that patient registration happens in 12 separate organizational units — duplication visible
  • Gap classifications: Added, Eliminated, Changed
  • ADD updated with Business Architecture content

Phase C: Data Architecture

What is happening: ANDH's data landscape is analysed and the Target Data Architecture defined. This is done BEFORE Application Architecture because applications must be designed to handle the data.

Baseline Data Architecture (AS-IS):

  • 6 separate Patient Record systems — no shared data model, no integration
  • No Master Patient Index (MPI) — patient identity is not managed centrally
  • No data governance — no defined data owners; no data quality standards enforced
  • Data quality assessment reveals: 34% of patient records have missing allergy information (Completeness violation); same patient appears with different spellings across systems (Uniqueness violation); lab results from 2019 still marked as "pending" (Timeliness violation)

Target Data Architecture (TO-BE):

  • Canonical Data Model established for core clinical entities: Patient, Encounter, Diagnosis, Medication, Lab Result, Imaging Study — all systems will use this CDM for data exchange
  • Master Patient Index (MPI) — Centralized MDM style: the MPI is the ONLY authoritative source of Patient identity; all systems read patient identity from the MPI
  • Data quality requirements added to ARS:
    • Patient allergy information: Completeness ≥ 99%
    • Patient identity: Uniqueness = 100% (no duplicate patient records)
    • Lab results: Timeliness — results available within 4 hours of completion
  • Data sovereignty documented: All patient data classified as "Sovereign Data" — must remain in KSA data centers; no processing outside KSA permitted
  • New data governance roles: Data Owner = Chief Medical Officer (accountable for clinical data); Patient Data Steward = new role (day-to-day quality management)

Gap Analysis (Phase C — Data):

Gap Classification
Canonical Data Model for clinical entities Added
Master Patient Index (MDM Centralized Style) Added
Data quality enforcement for Completeness/Uniqueness/Timeliness Added
6 separate Patient Record data models Eliminated (to be consolidated into CDM)
Data governance roles Added

Key TOGAF concepts in play:

  • Data Architecture always before Application Architecture (within Phase C)
  • CDM reduces N×(N-1)/2 transformations to N (6 systems × 5 / 2 = 15 transforms → 6 transforms)
  • MDM Centralized Style chosen because ANDH needs maximum data quality control
  • Data Sovereignty principle applied — crosses into Phase D technology constraints
  • Data Entity/Business Function Matrix (CRUD) shows which systems Create/own each clinical entity
  • 6 data quality dimensions — three violations found in baseline
  • ADD updated with Data Architecture content

Phase C: Application Architecture

What is happening: ANDH's 28 existing applications are assessed and the Target Application Architecture designed.

Application Portfolio Assessment (TIME Model):

Application Business Value Technical Health TIME Action
Core EMR (Electronic Medical Record) High — clinical backbone Poor — 15 years old, no vendor support Migrate Re-platform to modern EMR
Laboratory Information System High — critical clinical function Good — modern, well-supported Invest Add HL7 FHIR API interface
Radiology PACS High — imaging is critical Good — modern vendor-supported Invest Add FHIR interface
Pharmacy System High — patient safety critical Poor — runs on end-of-life OS Migrate Re-platform
6 legacy billing systems (one per region) Low — duplicated, one system sufficient Variable — some adequate, some poor Eliminate (5 of 6) + Invest (1 modern one) Consolidate to one billing platform
HR system Low — not strategic Adequate — vendor-supported Tolerate Keep running; no investment
3 duplicate appointment systems Low — duplicated function Adequate Eliminate (2) + Tolerate (1) Rationalize

Target Application Architecture:

  • New application: ANDH Patient Portal (web + mobile) — new, strategic → Invest
  • New application: Master Patient Index platform — implements the MDM architecture
  • New application: Enterprise Integration Platform (EIP) — implements Hub-and-Spoke / ESB pattern for connecting all clinical systems
  • New application: Clinical Decision Support Engine — AI-assisted; new capability
  • Modified: Core EMR re-platformed to a modern, cloud-capable EMR supporting HL7 FHIR APIs

Integration Architecture Decision: 28 systems with potential point-to-point connections = 28 × 27 / 2 = 378 connections. Architecture team recommends Hub-and-Spoke / ESB pattern:

  • After migration: 28 connections (one per system to the EIP hub)
  • Standard: HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) — Mandatory integration standard for all clinical data exchange
  • Architecture Decision Record ADR-001 created: "Adopt HL7 FHIR as the Mandatory clinical data exchange standard" — stored in Governance Log (Layer 6)

Gap Analysis (Phase C — Application):

Gap Classification
Patient Portal (web + mobile) Added
Master Patient Index platform Added
Enterprise Integration Platform (ESB) Added
Clinical Decision Support Engine Added
5 of 6 billing systems Eliminated
2 of 3 appointment systems Eliminated
Core EMR Changed (Migrate — re-platform)
378 point-to-point integrations Eliminated → replaced by ESB

Key TOGAF concepts in play:

  • TIME model applied to all 28 applications
  • Application/Business Function Matrix connecting Phase B capabilities to applications
  • ESB mathematical advantage demonstrated (378 → 28 connections)
  • HL7 FHIR as a domain-specific Mandatory standard (added to Standards Information Base, Layer 4)
  • ADR created for a major architectural decision
  • Service Contracts to be defined for all FHIR APIs (distinct from Architecture Contracts)
  • ADD updated with Application Architecture content

Phase D: Technology Architecture

What is happening: The infrastructure needed to support ANDH's new application landscape is designed.

Key Phase D decisions:

Cloud Deployment Model:

  • Patient data (clinical records) → Private Cloud on a KSA-based data centre (data sovereignty requirement from Phase B Architecture Principle and Phase C data classification)
  • Patient Portal and non-clinical workloads → Public Cloud (Azure KSA region — data residency confirmed within KSA)
  • DR: Hot Standby for clinical systems (patient safety critical; RTO < 15 minutes; RPO < 5 minutes)
  • DR: Warm Standby for administrative systems

High Availability:

  • Core EMR: Active-Active (any downtime is a patient safety risk)
  • Patient Portal: Active-Active (patient-facing; 99.9% availability in ARS)
  • HR and administrative systems: Active-Passive (brief failover acceptable)

Technology Standards (added to Standards Information Base):

Standard Category Scope
HL7 FHIR R4 Mandatory All clinical data exchange
OAuth 2.0 + PKCE Mandatory All API authentication
TLS 1.3 Mandatory All data in transit
Azure KSA Region Mandatory All cloud workloads
PostgreSQL 15 Recommended Relational databases
Kubernetes 1.28 Emerging Container orchestration (pilot phase)
Oracle 12c Retiring Legacy database platform; migrate by end of Year 2

Technology Reference Architecture (TRA) produced — maps TOGAF TRM categories to ANDH-specific products.

Gap Analysis (Phase D):

Gap Classification
KSA Private Cloud infrastructure for clinical systems Added
Azure KSA region configuration for portal Added
Hot Standby DR environment for clinical systems Added
Active-Active HA for Core EMR Changed (current is single-server)
Oracle 12c on legacy systems Eliminated (Retiring standard — migrate by Year 2)

Key TOGAF concepts in play:

  • Technology Architecture is LAST — it serves the applications and data
  • Data Sovereignty principle from Phase B Architecture Principles directly drives cloud deployment model
  • Cloud service model: Patient Portal = PaaS; Integration Platform = PaaS; Databases = IaaS
  • TRA produced and stored in Standards Information Base (Layer 4)
  • Technology standards classified (Mandatory/Recommended/Emerging/Retiring)
  • ADD now complete across all 4 domains

Phase E: Opportunities & Solutions

What is happening: All four domain Gap Analyses (Phase B, C Part 1, C Part 2, D) are consolidated into a coherent, sequenced roadmap.

Gap Consolidation: The architect identifies that several gaps are causally linked:

  • The "Unified Patient Record" Business gap requires the "Master Patient Index" Application gap, which requires the "CDM for clinical entities" Data gap, which requires the "KSA Private Cloud" Technology gap
  • These four gaps form a single Work Package: WP-001: Unified Patient Identity Foundation

Work Packages defined:

WP ID Work Package Name Related Gaps Domains
WP-001 Unified Patient Identity Foundation MPI platform + CDM + KSA Private Cloud + Data Governance roles Data, App, Tech
WP-002 Enterprise Integration Platform ESB deployment + HL7 FHIR onboarding of existing systems App, Tech
WP-003 Core EMR Re-platforming EMR migration to modern platform + HL7 FHIR interface App, Tech
WP-004 Patient Portal (Web + Mobile) Portal development + OAuth 2.0 integration + Azure KSA App, Tech
WP-005 Clinical Decision Support AI engine + integration with EMR + data lake App, Tech
WP-006 Legacy Rationalization Eliminate 5 billing systems; eliminate 2 appointment systems App
WP-007 Data Quality Programme Enforcement of completeness/uniqueness/timeliness standards Data

Transition Architectures defined:

  • Transition 1 (End of Year 1): WP-001 and WP-002 complete. All systems connected via ESB. MPI live. CDM in use for new data exchanges. Legacy Oracle migrated for clinical systems.
  • Transition 2 (End of Year 2): WP-003, WP-004, WP-007 complete. New EMR live. Patient Portal launched. Data quality standards enforced. Legacy billing rationalization done.
  • Target Architecture (End of Year 3): WP-005 complete. Clinical Decision Support live. All 28 systems integrated, rationalized, and compliant.

Architecture Roadmap v0.1 and Implementation Plan v0.1 produced.

Key TOGAF concepts in play:

  • Phase E is the CONSOLIDATION phase — not design, not planning in detail
  • Gaps from B, C, D consolidated here (NOT performed here for the first time)
  • Work Packages group related gaps into deliverable increments
  • Transition Architectures defined HERE (Phase E) — not Phase F
  • Cross-domain dependency analysis: WP-001 must come before WP-002 (you cannot build the ESB before the CDM is defined)
  • Roadmap v0.1 and Implementation Plan v0.1 — both "v0.1" because they need Phase F refinement

Phase F: Migration Planning

What is happening: The Phase E roadmap is refined with detailed planning, business value assigned to each Work Package, and Architecture Contracts produced.

Work Package prioritization:

WP Business Value Risk Priority
WP-001 (Unified Patient Identity) High (foundation for everything) High (complex data migration) 1st
WP-002 (Integration Platform) High (enables all other WPs) Medium 2nd
WP-006 (Legacy Rationalization) Medium (cost reduction) Low 3rd (can start in parallel)
WP-003 (EMR Re-platform) High (clinical safety) High 4th (after WP-001, WP-002)
WP-007 (Data Quality) High (compliance) Medium Parallel with WP-003
WP-004 (Patient Portal) High (patient experience) Medium 5th
WP-005 (Clinical Decision Support) High (strategic differentiator) High Last (requires all data foundation)

Architecture Roadmap finalized. Implementation and Migration Plan finalized.

Architecture Contracts produced:

  • Contract 1: For the WP-001 implementation team — specifies: CDM schema must be used; MPI must use Centralized MDM style; all data processing in KSA; Oracle 12c not permitted for new MPI platform; HL7 FHIR R4 compliance mandatory
  • Contract 2: For the WP-002 implementation team — specifies: HL7 FHIR R4 for all integrations; ESB pattern only; all interface specifications in Interface Catalog

Key TOGAF concepts in play:

  • Architecture Contracts are created HERE (Phase F) — not Phase G
  • Architecture Roadmap FINALIZED here — Phase E had v0.1
  • Business value assessment drives WP sequencing
  • Contracts are signed by both EA team and implementation team leads
  • Each contract references the ARS and the relevant sections of the ADD

Phase G: Implementation Governance

What is happening: WP-001 and WP-002 implementation is underway. The EA team monitors compliance.

Compliance Assessment — WP-001 (Unified Patient Identity): The implementation team has built the MPI. Phase G Compliance Assessment finds:

  • ✅ CDM schema used for all clinical entity exchanges — Conforms
  • ✅ MPI uses Centralized MDM style — Conforms
  • ✅ All processing in KSA data centre — Conforms
  • ❌ The team implemented MySQL 8 instead of the Mandatory PostgreSQL 15 — Non-conformant

Response to Non-conformance: The implementation team explains that the third-party MPI vendor only supports MySQL. The EA team reviews:

  • Option 1: Require the vendor to support PostgreSQL → Vendor says impossible without 18-month rebuild
  • Option 2: Dispensation Request → EA team recommends this
  • A Dispensation Request is submitted to the Architecture Review Committee
  • ARC grants a Dispensation: MySQL 8 is permitted for the MPI platform specifically, for 24 months, with a requirement to evaluate PostgreSQL-native MPI alternatives before renewal

Dispensation recorded in Governance Log (Layer 6).

Key TOGAF concepts in play:

  • Phase G uses Architecture Contracts (produced in Phase F) as baseline for compliance
  • Compliance Assessment produces a finding: Non-conformant (one item)
  • Three options for Non-conformance: Remediate / Dispensation / Architecture Change Request
  • Dispensation granted by Architecture Review Committee (Architecture Board equivalent)
  • Dispensation stored in Governance Log
  • Phase G does NOT create Architecture Contracts (Phase F does)

Phase H: Architecture Change Management

What is happening: 12 months after go-live of Transition Architecture 1, the following change triggers arrive:

Trigger 1 — Technology: The vendor of the Laboratory Information System announces it will discontinue the product in 18 months.

  • Classification: Technology Trigger (vendor discontinuation = EOL announcement)
  • Change type assessment: LIS is classified as Invest (high value, good tech). With discontinuation, it will become Migrate.
  • Recommendation: Incremental Change → loop back to Phase E/F to add a "LIS Re-platform" Work Package to the roadmap

Trigger 2 — Regulatory: Saudi NDMO issues a new directive requiring all healthcare organizations to classify patient data into three tiers and report data quality metrics quarterly.

  • Classification: Business/Regulatory Trigger
  • Change type assessment: This affects Business Architecture (new compliance process), Data Architecture (data classification tiers), and Application Architecture (reporting module needed)
  • Recommendation: Incremental Change → loop back to Phase E/F to add regulatory compliance Work Packages

Trigger 3 — Minor: The Patient Portal team requests a UI colour scheme change.

  • Classification: Not an architecture concern
  • Recommendation: Simplification Change — handled within Phase H; no ADM re-entry required

Key TOGAF concepts in play:

  • Phase H monitors DEPLOYED architecture — not in-progress implementations (that is Phase G)
  • Three trigger types: Business/Regulatory, Technology, Architecture
  • Three change types: Simplification (stay in H), Incremental (loop to E/F), Re-architecting (new Phase A)
  • Architecture Debt check: The Dispensation for MySQL has 12 months remaining — tracked in debt register
  • Phase H loops are how the ADM handles real-world change without restarting from scratch

Governance Walk-Through — End to End

The ANDH scenario shows the full governance chain:

  1. Architecture Principles (Preliminary) → govern every decision ("Patient Data Sovereignty" drives the entire cloud and DR strategy)
  2. Architecture Vision (Phase A) → high-level direction; stakeholder concerns mapped
  3. ADD (built in B, C, D; finalized F) → the master architecture document
  4. ARS (started A; updated B, C, D) → requirements baseline for compliance
  5. ADRs (Phase C) → architectural decisions with rationale, stored in Governance Log
  6. Architecture Roadmap (Phase E v0.1; Phase F final) → sequenced delivery plan
  7. Architecture Contracts (Phase F) → govern implementation
  8. Compliance Assessments (Phase G) → check delivery against contracts
  9. Dispensation (Phase G → ARC) → formally accept MySQL exception
  10. Phase H triggers (post go-live) → manage ongoing change

Every document, every governance action, every architectural decision in the ANDH scenario maps to a specific TOGAF element. This is the integrated TOGAF system in action.

Key Takeaway for Days 1–2

The ANDH scenario shows TOGAF as a flowing system, not a list of facts. Preliminary sets up governance. Phase A scopes and sponsors. B/C/D design each domain, each updating the ADD and ARS. Phase E consolidates all gaps into Work Packages and Transition Architectures. Phase F adds contracts and finalizes the roadmap. Phase G checks compliance and manages deviations. Phase H monitors and adapts. Every document connects to the phase that created it. Every decision traces to a principle, a requirement, or a stakeholder concern. When you see a scenario question on the exam, ask: "Where in the ANDH story does this fit?"

Day 3 (Wednesday): Practice Exam 1

Instructions: 55 minutes. Close all notes. Answer all 40 questions. Do not check answers until you have finished all 40. Target: 65%+ (26/40) on this first attempt — your score will improve after gap analysis and targeted re-study.

After completing, use the Answer Key and the Day 4 Gap Analysis Framework to understand every wrong answer.

Q1. What formal document triggers the start of Phase A in a new TOGAF ADM cycle?

A) Architecture Vision
B) Statement of Architecture Work
C) Request for Architecture Work
D) Architecture Principles

Answer: C — A Request for Architecture Work is submitted by the Architecture Sponsor to the Architecture Board / EA team to initiate a specific architecture project. It triggers Phase A. The Statement of Architecture Work is a Phase A OUTPUT (not a trigger). The Architecture Vision is also a Phase A output.

Q2. TOGAF describes the ADM as "iterative." Which of the following is the MOST accurate description of what this means?

A) Each phase must be completely finished before the next can begin, with no going back
B) The ADM can be repeated at different levels of detail (Strategic, Segment, Capability), and phases can be revisited when new information requires it
C) Only Phases A and H are iterative; the design phases B, C, D are linear
D) Iteration means running the same phase twice in identical fashion to validate results

Answer: B — ADM iteration means three things: within-cycle iteration (returning to earlier phases when new information requires revision), cycle iteration at three landscape levels (Strategic, Segment, Capability), and Phase H change-driven re-entry. The ADM is explicitly not a linear one-way flow.

Q3. (Scenario) A major Saudi bank has completed Phases B, C (both parts), and D. The architecture team now sits down to answer: "Given everything we know about business gaps, data gaps, application gaps, and technology gaps — what is the best sequence for closing these gaps, and what intermediate operational states will the organization need?" Which phase is beginning?

A) Phase F — Migration Planning
B) Phase G — Implementation Governance
C) Phase H — Architecture Change Management
D) Phase E — Opportunities and Solutions

Answer: D — Phase E: the phase that consolidates all domain gap analyses, identifies Work Packages, defines Transition Architectures, and creates the Architecture Roadmap v0.1. The description — "consolidating gaps and determining sequence and intermediate states" — is the precise purpose of Phase E. Phase F takes Phase E's outputs and adds detailed planning and Architecture Contracts.

Q4. Which of the following is a formal output of Phase F (Migration Planning) that is NOT produced in Phase E?

A) Architecture Roadmap v0.1
B) Transition Architectures
C) Architecture Contracts
D) Work Packages

Answer: C — Architecture Contracts are produced in Phase F. Phase E produces: Architecture Roadmap v0.1, Transition Architectures, Work Packages, Implementation Plan v0.1. Phase F finalizes the roadmap, finalizes the implementation plan, and — uniquely — creates Architecture Contracts. This is one of the most commonly tested distinctions.

Q5. (Scenario) Al-Noor Digital Health has just completed a full ADM cycle for its enterprise transformation. The CIO now wants to run a separate, more detailed ADM cycle focused specifically on the Clinical Data domain — implementing the data governance roles, CDM, and MPI identified in the enterprise cycle. What type of ADM application is this?

A) Within-cycle iteration — returning to Phase C for more detail
B) Cycle iteration at the Segment Architecture level — a focused ADM cycle for one domain/program within the enterprise architecture
C) Phase H Re-architecting change — the clinical data architecture requires redesign
D) Part III technique — Capability-Based Planning applied to the clinical data domain

Answer: B — Segment Architecture cycle: a separate ADM cycle scoped to a specific part of the enterprise (the Clinical Data domain), operating within the constraints set by the Strategic (enterprise-wide) ADM cycle. This is the second level of the three-level landscape hierarchy (Strategic → Segment → Capability).

Q6. The Architecture Requirements Specification (ARS) is described as a "living document." What does this mean in the context of the ADM?

A) It is written informally and does not need to be formally approved
B) It is created once in Phase A and never changed after that
C) It is created in Phase A and continuously updated in every subsequent phase as new requirements are discovered, until it is finalized in Phase F
D) It is replaced by the Architecture Definition Document once Phase B begins

Answer: C — The ARS is created initially in Phase A with high-level requirements and updated in every subsequent phase as more detailed requirements are discovered. Phase B adds business requirements; Phase C adds data and application requirements; Phase D adds technology requirements. It is the living requirements baseline against which Phase G compliance is measured.

Q7. (Scenario) During Phase B at ANDH, the architect identifies that the Business Capability Map shows "Population Health Analytics" as a required capability in the Target Architecture. This capability does not exist today — no process, no system, no role, and no budget currently supports it. How is this gap classified?

A) Changed gap — the capability exists but needs to be improved
B) Eliminated gap — the capability will not be carried forward
C) Retained gap — unchanged between baseline and target
D) Added gap — the capability exists in the target but not in the baseline

Answer: D — Added gap: a capability (or any other architectural element) that exists in the Target Architecture but does not exist in the Baseline Architecture. This must be created. An "Added" gap always generates at least one Work Package in Phase E.

Q8. In TOGAF, Architecture Principles have four formal components. Which combination correctly lists all four?

A) Name, Description, Owner, Date
B) Name, Statement, Rationale, Implications
C) Name, Priority, Author, Category
D) Title, Definition, Examples, Exceptions

Answer: B — The four formal components of an Architecture Principle are: Name (short label), Statement (concise description of the principle), Rationale (why this principle is important), and Implications (what following this principle means for the organization). This is a direct factual question from the TOGAF specification.

Q9. (Scenario) An architect is reviewing ANDH's Architecture Repository. She finds the following items stored in the repository: the HL7 FHIR R4 standard (classified as Mandatory), a list of ISO 27001 controls adopted by ANDH, and the Technology Reference Architecture mapping TRM categories to ANDH's specific products. In which layer of the Architecture Repository are these items stored?

A) Layer 3 — Architecture Landscape
B) Layer 4 — Standards Information Base
C) Layer 5 — Reference Library
D) Layer 6 — Governance Log

Answer: B — Layer 4, Standards Information Base: stores all approved standards — technology standards with their Mandatory/Recommended/Emerging/Retiring classification, external standards (ISO, IEEE, HL7), and the organization's Technology Reference Architecture. Layer 3 stores actual architectures. Layer 5 stores reference models and reusable patterns. Layer 6 stores governance records.

Q10. (Scenario) An ANDH architect documents the decision to use HL7 FHIR R4 as the Mandatory clinical data exchange standard. The document captures: the context (28 systems with incompatible formats), the decision (adopt HL7 FHIR R4), the rationale (open standard, widely supported in healthcare, enables interoperability), the rejected alternatives (custom XML format — rejected for lock-in; HL7 v2 — rejected as outdated), and the consequences (positive: interoperability; negative: team training required). Where is this document stored?

A) Layer 4 — Standards Information Base
B) Layer 3 — Architecture Landscape
C) Layer 6 — Governance Log
D) Layer 5 — Reference Library

Answer: C — This is an Architecture Decision Record (ADR). ADRs — with their Title, Status, Context, Decision, Rationale, and Consequences — are stored in the Governance Log (Layer 6). The standard itself (HL7 FHIR R4) is stored in Layer 4, but the DECISION RECORD about adopting it goes in Layer 6.

Q11. A Phase G Compliance Assessment finds that a delivered patient portal uses the correct authentication approach, meets all stated performance requirements, and follows the specified integration patterns. However, one non-critical feature specified in the Architecture Contract — a preference panel for accessibility settings — was not implemented due to time pressure. All clinically critical features are present. Which compliance level BEST applies?

A) Fully Conformant
B) Conformant
C) Compliant
D) Non-conformant

Answer: B — Conformant: the solution meets the architecture in all significant respects, with minor, documented deviations (the missing non-critical accessibility panel). Fully Conformant requires meeting every specified aspect without deviation. A minor, non-critical omission documented and acknowledged = Conformant, not Fully Conformant.

Q12. (Scenario) The ANDH Architecture Review Committee (equivalent to Architecture Board) discovers that a project team implemented a custom proprietary integration format between the Pharmacy system and the Core EMR, bypassing the HL7 FHIR R4 Mandatory standard specified in the Architecture Contract. The team says the vendor's proprietary format was "faster to implement." What is the compliance level and what options does the ARC have?

A) Compliant — the integration works, which is what matters
B) Consistent — the team used similar integration concepts
C) Non-conformant — actively conflicts with the Architecture Contract; options: (1) require the team to implement HL7 FHIR R4, (2) grant a Dispensation with a remediation deadline, (3) submit an Architecture Change Request if FHIR R4 itself needs revision
D) Irrelevant — integration format choices are not an architecture concern

Answer: C — Non-conformant: the solution actively violates the Architecture Contract (Mandatory HL7 FHIR R4 standard). "Faster to implement" is not a valid justification — it is the basis for a Dispensation Request at most. The ARC's three options: Remediate, Dispensation (with deadline), Architecture Change Request (only if the standard itself is wrong, not applicable here).

Q13. Which of the following BEST describes the relationship between the Architecture Landscape and the Enterprise Continuum?

A) They are the same concept described from different perspectives
B) The Enterprise Continuum is a classification system for architecture assets; the Architecture Landscape is a representation of the actual architectures an organization currently has (Baseline) and is developing (Target), organized at Strategic, Segment, and Capability levels
C) The Architecture Landscape is stored in the Enterprise Continuum
D) The Enterprise Continuum contains only external reference architectures; the Architecture Landscape contains only internal architectures

Answer: B — Enterprise Continuum: a classification method for organizing architecture assets on a spectrum from generic to organization-specific. Architecture Landscape: the actual architectures of THIS organization, organized at three levels. They are distinct concepts. The Landscape is stored in Layer 3 of the Architecture Repository. The Continuum is the classification scheme that organizes what is stored.

Q14. (Scenario) ANDH's Chief Medical Officer is concerned about clinical patient safety — specifically which systems contain medication information, which systems can modify medication records, and what the handoff process is between systems when prescriptions are filled. What combination of artifacts would BEST address these concerns?

A) Business Capability Map + Organizational Map
B) Data Entity/Business Function Matrix (showing CRUD for Medication entity) + Application Communication Diagram + Process Flow Diagram for prescription workflow
C) Technology Standards Catalog + Infrastructure Diagram
D) Architecture Vision + Statement of Architecture Work

Answer: B — The CMO's concerns map directly to: Data Entity/Business Function Matrix (which system Creates/owns Medication data, which Read it, which can Update it) + Application Communication Diagram (how systems exchange medication information) + Process Flow Diagram (the clinical workflow for prescriptions). This is the concern → viewpoint → view chain applied: CMO's patient safety concern → clinical data safety viewpoint → these specific artifacts.

Q15. Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the Technical Reference Model (TRM)?

A) A detailed blueprint for how applications should integrate with each other
B) A taxonomy of generic technology service categories organized into the Application Platform and Communications Infrastructure — used as a basis for Phase D technology classification
C) An organization-specific catalog of approved technology products
D) A model showing how TOGAF phases connect to technology decisions

Answer: B — The TRM is a TAXONOMY of technology service categories — a vocabulary for describing technology, not a prescription. It has two main components: the Application Platform (service categories: Data Management, Security, Integration, etc.) and the Communications Infrastructure. It is used in Phase D as a starting point that organizations customize into their own Technology Reference Architecture (TRA). B is the most accurate description.

Q16. What is the primary difference between the TOGAF Technical Reference Model (TRM) and the Integrated Information Infrastructure Reference Model (III-RM)?

A) The TRM is for technology; the III-RM is for business processes
B) The TRM provides a taxonomy of all technology service categories; the III-RM provides a specific architectural pattern showing how Business Applications, Infrastructure Applications, and the Application Platform work together to enable boundaryless information flow
C) They are alternative names for the same reference model
D) The TRM is used in Phase B; the III-RM is used in Phase H

Answer: B — TRM = taxonomy of technology service CATEGORIES (what types of technology exist). III-RM = specific ARCHITECTURE PATTERN for integrated enterprise information infrastructure (how the pieces connect). The III-RM answers "how should we structure our application and infrastructure landscape to enable seamless information flow?" The TRM answers "what categories of technology service exist?" Both are Foundation Architecture assets (Layer 5 of the Repository).

Q17. (Scenario) ANDH's CFO requests a presentation showing "where we are spending money on technology, which systems are strategic, and which are candidates for retirement." An architect creates a diagram showing all 28 applications placed into four quadrants based on business value and technical health. What is this diagram?

A) Application Communication Diagram
B) Application/Technology Matrix
C) TIME Model Application Portfolio Assessment diagram
D) Platform Decomposition Diagram

Answer: C — The TIME Model Application Portfolio Assessment presents applications in four quadrants (Tolerate, Invest, Migrate, Eliminate) based on Business Value and Technical Health. This is exactly what the CFO is asking for — a portfolio rationalization view. The Application Communication Diagram shows integrations. The Application/Technology Matrix shows which apps run on which tech. Platform Decomposition shows technology stack layers.

Q18. In TOGAF's Content Framework, which of the following is the CORRECT classification of a "Technology Standards Catalog"?

A) Deliverable — it is formally contracted and signed off
B) Diagram — it is a visual representation
C) Catalog — it is an inventory of standards organized as a list
D) Matrix — it shows relationships between two sets of items

Answer: C — Catalog: an inventory of architecture elements, organized as a structured list. A Technology Standards Catalog lists technology standards and their attributes (name, category, version, scope). It is not a matrix (no cross-referencing two sets). It is not a diagram (not visual). It is a deliverable component but classified as an artifact type = Catalog.

Q19. (Scenario) An architect is explaining the value of the Business Function/Organization Matrix to a sceptical CFO who says "why do we need yet another document?" The architect says: "This matrix immediately shows us something we couldn't see before." What does it reveal that justifies its creation?

A) It shows which systems are the most expensive to maintain
B) It reveals which business functions are performed by which organizational units — making duplication visible (same function performed by multiple units) and separation-of-duties risks visible (sensitive functions performed by one unit)
C) It shows the reporting hierarchy between executives
D) It shows which technology platforms support which business units

Answer: B — The Business Function/Organization Matrix cross-references Functions (rows) with Organizational Units (columns). The resulting view makes two things immediately visible: (1) Duplication — multiple units performing the same function, indicating consolidation opportunity; (2) Separation-of-duties risk — sensitive functions (e.g., "Authorize Payment" + "Process Payment") performed by the same unit. This is the matrix's unique value.

Q20. (Scenario) ANDH is designing the MDM strategy for the Patient entity. The Clinical Director insists that the legacy systems in 6 hospitals cannot be modified. However, a central record for each patient must be established. Clinicians in all hospitals must be able to find any patient by searching a single system, regardless of which hospital originally registered them. The legacy systems will remain the record of truth for their own patients during a long transition. Which MDM style fits?

A) Centralized Style — the central store is the only authority
B) Registry Style — a central store holds cross-references; legacy systems remain authoritative and unchanged
C) Consolidation Style — data extracted to a central read-only store for reporting
D) Coexistence Style — central and legacy stores are both authoritative

Answer: B — Registry Style: the legacy systems cannot be modified (rules out Centralized and Coexistence which require integration). A central Registry stores only patient ID cross-references (which hospital has which patient ID), allowing search across all hospitals without touching legacy data. Legacy systems remain authoritative for their own records. Note: the scenario said "cannot be modified" — this is the key constraint that selects Registry.

Q21. What is the correct ADM phase in which the Architecture Definition Document (ADD) is FIRST created (not just updated)?

A) Phase A — Architecture Vision
B) Phase B — Business Architecture
C) Phase E — Opportunities and Solutions
D) Phase F — Migration Planning

Answer: B — The ADD is first created in Phase B when the Business Architecture baseline and target are documented. Phase A produces the Architecture Vision and the initial ARS, but the ADD begins in Phase B. It is then updated in Phase C (Data Architecture added, then Application Architecture), Phase D (Technology Architecture added), and finalized in Phase F.

Q22. (Scenario) During Phase H monitoring at ANDH, the architecture team discovers that the vendor for the Core Laboratory Information System (LIS) has announced the product will reach End of Life in 14 months. The LIS is currently classified as Invest (high value, good technology). How should Phase H handle this?

A) No action required — Phase H only monitors for business triggers, not technology events
B) This is a Technology Trigger; since the LIS is high-value and its technical health will drop to poor at EOL, the appropriate response is an Incremental Change — loop back to Phase E/F to add an LIS re-platform Work Package to the Architecture Roadmap
C) Immediately start a new Phase A cycle for the LIS re-platforming
D) Grant a Dispensation to allow the LIS to continue past its EOL date

Answer: B — Technology Trigger (vendor EOL announcement). The LIS is high-value (current TIME = Invest), but EOL will make technical health poor → it must Migrate. This is a significant but scoped change (one application) = Incremental Change → loop to Phase E/F to add the re-platform Work Package. A new Phase A cycle (Re-architecting) would be warranted only if this required redesigning the entire enterprise architecture. A Dispensation applies to compliance deviations, not technology lifecycle decisions.

Q23. Which of the following CORRECTLY describes a Viewpoint in TOGAF?

A) A specific diagram created for a particular stakeholder showing one aspect of the architecture
B) A specification or template that defines the information to include, the notation to use, and the modelling techniques to apply when creating a view for a particular concern
C) A perspective held by a stakeholder about the architecture
D) An informal summary of the architecture produced for executive communication

Answer: B — A Viewpoint is a SPECIFICATION (template) that defines: what information to include, what notation to use, and what modelling technique to apply — so that consistent Views can be created for the same concern across multiple architecture projects. A View is the instance created by applying the Viewpoint to a specific architecture. C describes a "concern," not a viewpoint. A describes a "view," not a viewpoint.

Q24. (Scenario) ANDH's architecture team creates a "Clinical Safety Viewpoint" that specifies: "This viewpoint addresses the CISO and CMO's concerns about patient data protection and medication safety. It shows: (1) data classification of all entities, (2) access controls per system, (3) medication update authority per system. Notation: combination of Data Security Diagram and Data Entity Matrix. Audience: CISO, CMO, Compliance team." They then apply this viewpoint to produce representations for the current architecture AND the target architecture. What has been produced?

A) One Viewpoint; two Views
B) Two Viewpoints; two Views
C) One View; two Viewpoints
D) One Viewpoint; one View

Answer: A — One Viewpoint (the Clinical Safety Viewpoint specification — the template), applied to two different architectures (current and target) to produce two Views. A Viewpoint is reusable; Views are instances. The same Viewpoint can produce many Views for many different architectures or at different points in time.

Q25. An organization decides to customize TOGAF for its specific context. Which of the following CAN be customized in the Preliminary Phase?

A) The direction of the ADM cascade (Technology before Business is an acceptable customization)
B) TOGAF terminology — replacing "Architecture Board" with the organization's existing governance body name, and adapting phase names to match existing processes
C) The requirement for stakeholder management — organizations that are small can skip stakeholder identification
D) The requirement for architecture governance — governance is optional for small organizations

Answer: B — Terminology and governance structure names CAN be tailored. What CANNOT be changed: the cascade direction (Business always before Technology), the governance principle (architecture decisions must be reviewed), and stakeholder management (always required). Options A, C, and D each describe something that is a non-negotiable core of TOGAF that cannot be removed.

Q26. (Scenario) A new ANDH project team is about to begin implementing WP-003 (Core EMR Re-platform). The project manager asks the EA team: "What document tells us exactly what we need to build, what standards we must comply with, what technology we must use, and how compliance will be measured?" Which document is the project manager asking for?

A) Statement of Architecture Work
B) Architecture Vision
C) Architecture Contract
D) Implementation and Migration Plan

Answer: C — Architecture Contract (Phase F output): the governance agreement between the EA team and the implementation team, specifying WHAT must be built, WHAT standards apply, WHAT quality requirements must be met, and HOW compliance will be assessed in Phase G. The SoAW governs architecture development (not implementation). The Architecture Vision is high-level direction (not implementation specification).

Q27. In TOGAF Part III (ADM Guidelines and Techniques), the "Business Transformation Readiness Assessment" technique is used to:

A) Assess whether the organization's technology infrastructure is ready for deployment
B) Assess the organization's readiness and willingness to undergo business change — including factors like leadership commitment, culture, available funding, and change management capability
C) Evaluate whether the architecture team has the skills to complete the ADM
D) Measure the gap between current and target business capabilities

Answer: B — Business Transformation Readiness Assessment (Part III technique, used in Phase E): evaluates the organization's ability to execute a transformation. Key factors assessed include: leadership sponsorship, change culture, available budget, programme management capability, staff readiness, and communication effectiveness. This is distinct from Architecture Capability Maturity (which assesses the EA practice) and Gap Analysis (which identifies architectural differences).

Q28. (Scenario) ANDH's EA team is reviewing the Enterprise Continuum to find reusable architecture assets for the clinical data integration architecture. They find a healthcare industry reference architecture (BIAN-equivalent for healthcare — called HIA) that defines standard clinical service domains. According to the Enterprise Continuum concept, at which level does this HIA reference architecture sit, and how should ANDH use it?

A) Foundation Architecture level — use it unchanged
B) Organization-Specific Architecture level — it already represents ANDH's specific architecture
C) Industry Architecture level — use it as a starting point; customize it toward the Organization-Specific level by adding ANDH's specific constraints, regulatory requirements, and technology choices
D) Common Systems Architecture level — it applies to all organizations with similar types of systems

Answer: C — Industry Architecture level: a reference architecture specific to an industry (healthcare) but applicable to multiple organizations within it. The correct Enterprise Continuum usage: take the Industry Architecture as a starting point and customize it (moving right along the continuum toward Organization-Specific) by adding ANDH's Saudi regulatory requirements, specific patient data sovereignty constraints, and technology choices. Never use Industry Architecture unchanged — it is a starting point.

Q29. (Scenario) Two architects at ANDH are discussing integration options for connecting 12 clinical systems in real time. Architect A says: "We should use a central ESB — one hub that all systems connect to, so we have N connections instead of N×(N-1)/2." Architect B says: "For clinical systems with real-time patient safety alerts, we need each system to publish events when something critical happens, and all interested systems automatically receive those alerts without the originating system waiting." Are these patterns the same or different, and if different, which should be used for real-time safety alerts?

A) They are the same pattern; the ESB handles both routing and events
B) They are different patterns; for real-time safety alerts where the source system must not wait for responses, the Event-Driven / Publish-Subscribe pattern (Architect B) is more appropriate than a synchronous ESB
C) Architect A's ESB is always superior; Architect B's approach does not exist in TOGAF
D) Both are wrong; point-to-point is the only reliable pattern for patient safety systems

Answer: B — These are different patterns: ESB/Hub-and-Spoke routes messages synchronously through a central hub (good for orchestration and transformation); Event-Driven / Pub-Sub publishes events asynchronously to subscribers (good for one-to-many broadcast where the source must not wait). For "real-time safety alerts where the system must not wait" — this is the definition of Pub-Sub's use case. The ESB could work but adds latency through the hub.

Q30. Which of the following statements about Architecture Principles is FALSE?

A) Architecture Principles are established in the Preliminary Phase
B) Each Architecture Principle has four components: Name, Statement, Rationale, and Implications
C) Architecture Principles can be overridden by a project team if they believe a principle is not relevant to their project
D) Architecture Principles govern all subsequent ADM phases and architecture decisions

Answer: C — FALSE. Architecture Principles CANNOT be unilaterally overridden by a project team. If a project believes a principle conflicts with its requirements, it must seek a formal Dispensation or Architecture Change Request from the Architecture Board. Principles represent enterprise-wide governance commitments. Options A, B, and D are all true statements about Architecture Principles.

Q31. (Scenario) ANDH's CISO asks: "We need to understand, for every piece of patient data in our new architecture, where it originated, every system it passed through, every transformation applied to it, and who accessed it — for both compliance audits and data breach investigation." C) Application Communication Diagram — shows which applications communicate with which

Answer: B — Data Lineage Diagram: backward-looking historical audit trail of where data came from, what transformations it went through, and who touched it. This is the compliance and breach investigation tool. The Data Flow Diagram shows current operational flows (architecture design tool, not audit tool). Data Lineage is the specific artifact for the CISO's audit and forensic requirement.

Q32. (Scenario) An architect is presenting the ANDH target architecture to a group of stakeholders. For the CEO, she shows a "Business Value Realization" view focusing on capability changes and business outcomes. For the CISO, she shows a "Clinical Data Security" view focusing on data classification and access controls. For the CFO, she shows a "Technology Investment" view focusing on portfolio rationalization and costs. These three representations are all derived from the same underlying architecture. What TOGAF concept explains this practice?

A) Architecture Partitioning — dividing the architecture into separate domains
B) Each stakeholder has a different Concern; each Concern maps to a different Viewpoint; each Viewpoint produces a different View of the same underlying architecture
C) The Architecture Landscape has three levels; each executive sees a different level
D) Different phases of the ADM produce different architecture representations

Q33. (Scenario) ANDH is using ITIL for IT service management alongside TOGAF. The WP-001 implementation (Unified Patient Identity Foundation) has completed Phase G compliance successfully. Before the system goes live in production, the IT operations team requires that the change be formally assessed by their Change Advisory Board (CAB). The ANDH EA team says "but we already did a Phase G compliance review." Who is correct, and why?

A) The EA team is correct — Phase G compliance supersedes ITIL Change Management
B) Both are correct and serve different purposes: Phase G Compliance Assessment confirms the system meets the Architecture Contract; ITIL Change Management CAB approval controls the risk of deploying the change to the production environment. Both are required before go-live.
C) ITIL Change Management supersedes Phase G — only one review is needed
D) Neither is required — the implementation team can deploy directly to production

Answer: B — Both serve different purposes and both are required. Phase G = architectural compliance (does the system do what the architecture said?). ITIL Change Management = production deployment risk (is it safe to deploy now, given production dependencies and operational risks?). These are complementary governance gates, not redundant ones.

Q34. The TOGAF Content Framework distinguishes between Deliverables, Artifacts, and Building Blocks. Which of the following is a DELIVERABLE (not an artifact)?

A) Business Capability Map
B) Data Flow Diagram
C) Architecture Definition Document (ADD)
D) Application/Business Function Matrix

Answer: C — The Architecture Definition Document (ADD) is a Deliverable — it is formally contracted, formally reviewed, and formally signed off. The Business Capability Map, Data Flow Diagram, and Application/Business Function Matrix are all Artifacts — they describe aspects of the architecture but are components within deliverables, not deliverables themselves. Deliverables are the formally committed outputs; Artifacts are the content inside them.

Q35. (Scenario) ANDH has adopted the following approach: The EA team maintains an updated architecture picture at least 6 months ahead of the implementation teams. When the implementation teams complete a Programme Increment, they consume some of the architectural foundation. If the teams ever reach a point where the architecture ahead of them is not defined, the EA team must urgently close the gap. This approach ensures Agile teams are never blocked by architectural unknowns. What concept is being described?

A) Phase E Work Package management
B) Transition Architecture sequencing
C) Architecture Runway — EA maintains architectural foundations ahead of delivery teams so teams always have a defined structure to build within
D) Architecture Debt management — EA pre-emptively prevents accumulation of architectural unknowns

Answer: C — Architecture Runway (SAFe concept adopted in TOGAF Agile contexts): the EA team maintains architectural decisions ahead of delivery teams, ensuring teams always have a proven foundation to build on. "Teams consuming the runway" and "EA must extend the runway before teams reach its end" are the defining characteristics of the Architecture Runway concept.

Q36. Which ADM phase produces the FIRST complete, integrated Architecture Roadmap — showing all Work Packages, Transition Architectures, and the sequenced path from Baseline to Target Architecture across all four domains?

A) Phase D — Technology Architecture
B) Phase E — Opportunities and Solutions (Architecture Roadmap v0.1)
C) Phase F — Migration Planning (Architecture Roadmap, finalized)
D) Phase G — Implementation Governance

Answer: B — Phase E produces the FIRST complete Architecture Roadmap (v0.1). This is the first time all four domain gap analyses are consolidated into a single integrated roadmap. Phase F finalizes it (removes the "v0.1") and adds Architecture Contracts. Phase D produces only the Technology domain's gap analysis — not an integrated cross-domain roadmap.

Q37. (Scenario) A hospital group is implementing TOGAF alongside DAMA-DMBOK. The TOGAF Phase C Data Architecture team has defined: a Canonical Data Model for clinical entities, data quality requirements (Patient Completeness ≥ 99%, Lab Result Timeliness ≤ 4 hours), and has specified Centralized MDM for the Patient entity. The DAMA team is now asked to implement these. Which DAMA-DMBOK Knowledge Areas are primarily responsible for each element?

B) CDM → Data Integration & Interoperability; Data Quality Requirements → Data Quality KA; Centralized MDM → Reference & Master Data KA

D) DAMA-DMBOK does not address these — they remain TOGAF architecture decisions

MDM Centralized Style → Reference & Master Data (DAMA KA 8 — implementing the authoritative master record). TOGAF defines the WHAT; DAMA implements the HOW.

Q38. Which of the following BEST describes the role of Architecture Partitioning in the Enterprise Continuum?

A) Partitioning means dividing architecture work by phase — one phase per team
B) Partitioning is the practice of dividing an architecture into manageable pieces based on subject matter, time period, or organizational scope — enabling different teams to work on different segments without creating conflicts
C) Partitioning means splitting the Architecture Repository into separate databases

C) Coexistence Style
D) Consolidation Style

Answer: C — Coexistence Style: both the central MDM platform AND the operational systems are authoritative in their respective domains, with bidirectional synchronization.
